title: Say it the way you'd say it in the chair, and fill the quiet days
thesis: Week 1 produced three posts and none of them went up. The reason was not the formats — the audience never saw them. It was that the tone read as written copy rather than as Sha talking, and the files never reached her phone. So week 2 keeps the formats, rewrites the voice into speech (contractions, first person, one reader), and hands the images over directly. The second job is Wednesday and Thursday: those are the quiet days this week, so one post is built to drive bookings onto them and the other two carry it. No discount anywhere — scarcity and a better appointment, not money off.
projection: The account sat still this week at 176 followers and 7.48% average engagement, because nothing was published — that is a flat line from an unrun week, not a decline. If all three go up, the growth model puts the target at roughly 183 followers by 24 Aug (~4% on 176) and the bar to beat is 7.48% average engagement. The one thing to change is the voice: every caption here uses contractions and speaks to one person, because 'tone felt off' was the stated reason week 1 stayed in the folder. What this sets up for next week is the first real signal the system has ever had — three published posts whose engagement can be scored against a known baseline, and an answer to whether the quiet-day post actually moved bookings onto a Wednesday. If Wednesday is still empty next week, the problem is demand rather than the caption, and the honest thing will be to say so instead of running it again.

posts.title: Saturday isn't the best day for a big colour
posts.imageAlt: Cream card with the line 'Saturday is the best day for a big colour' struck through in gold, answered by 'The chair is the same. The room around it is not.' Below, two rows: mid-week the salon is quiet, and this week Wednesday and Thursday are the quiet ones.
posts.whyItWorks: This is the post that has a job beyond reach: Wednesday and Thursday are empty and an empty chair is money already lost. It fills them without discounting, which matters because a price cut to fill a day teaches a 20-year specialist's audience to wait for one. Instead it reframes the quiet day as the better appointment, which is true — a three-and-a-half hour colour genuinely is a worse experience in a salon running flat out. Striking through a belief the reader holds is also the strongest opening this account has: the myth shape reads as news rather than advice, and news gets forwarded.

caption.hook: Saturday isn't the best time for a big colour. Wednesday is.
caption.body:
I know the weekend feels like the sensible pick. But a balayage is three and a half hours in the chair, and on a Saturday the whole salon is flat out around you.

Mid-week it's calm. You get the full appointment at your own pace, and there's time to talk properly about what we're doing before I start mixing.

Wednesday and Thursday are the quiet ones this week.

posts.title: A lived-in blonde starts at $340
posts.imageAlt: Dark card reading 'A lived-in blonde starts at $340', with a breakdown of hand-painted balayage, toner and blow wave, and a note that Wednesday and Thursday are the quiet ones this week.
posts.whyItWorks: Nobody local publishes a number, so a price post is the most screenshotted and forwarded thing a service business can put out — the person who decides is often not the person who saw it. It also kills the 'how much is a balayage?' DM before it is sent, which is the DM that sits unanswered for two days and loses the booking. Timing is the other half: spring starts on 1 September, so this runs in the fortnight when someone is deciding whether to walk into the season with the colour they have been carrying since June. It points at the $340 band rather than the $45 one, which is what makes filling a Wednesday actually worth filling.

caption.hook: Spring is two weeks away and your colour is still on winter settings.
caption.body:
Winter does a specific thing to colour. Heating running constantly, showers hotter than they should be, hair under a beanie half the week — by August it has all pulled the tone flat.

A lived-in blonde starts at $340. That's foils placed where the light actually hits, a toner to sort the tone, and a blow wave. Three and a half hours, and it's built to grow out softly so you're not back in six weeks.

If you want to walk into September looking like the season changed with you, the next fortnight is when to do it.

posts.title: Four things winter did to your hair
posts.imageAlt: Dark card headed 'Four things winter did to your hair', listing ducted heating pulling moisture out, showers hotter than lukewarm, friction where a beanie sits, and treatments skipped until summer.
posts.whyItWorks: Saves are weighted six times a like in the engine's own scoring, and a numbered list is the only format that is useless unless you keep it. This one is also diagnostic rather than instructional — it asks the reader to identify which of the four is theirs, which turns a save into a DM and a DM into a consultation. It sells the treatment work and the K18 add-on without an offer in it, and it sets up the rebook by giving her something specific to ask about when they next sit down.

caption.hook: Winter has done four things to your hair. Only one of them is obvious.
caption.body:
Save this one before your next appointment.

The dryness you can see is the last thing to show up — the rest has been building since June, and it changes how your hair takes colour.

Tell me which of these sounds like you and I'll change what I do in the chair. If the ends are fragile, K18 goes in before the lift, not after.

videoGuides.title: Three reasons your colour looks flat right now
videoGuides.difficulty: Easiest. No client needed. Phone propped against the mirror, you talking to camera, one take between appointments.

copyThis.creator: Freddie.yeah
copyThis.whatItIs: A stylist to camera opening on "Never blonde enough? Here are 3 reasons why", then counting the reasons off with each one captioned on screen as it is said.
copyThis.whyItCopies: This is the numbered-explainer format, and it is the single most repeated shape among colourists getting reach right now. It works because the opening line is a problem the viewer already has, so they stay for the diagnosis. Nothing in it needs a client, a second person, or an edit — which matters, because no time was the reason last week's guides never got filmed.
howToCopy: Watch it once at full speed, then once with the sound off. The second pass is the one that matters — notice she never introduces herself and the first frame is already the claim.
Prop your phone at eye height against the mirror. Stand so the salon is behind you, not a blank wall.
Say your version of her opening line straight down the lens, flatly: "Three reasons your colour looks flat right now."
Count the three on your fingers as you say them: heating drying the cuticle, showers too hot washing the toner out early, and stretching to eight or nine weeks because nobody sees it under a beanie.
Stop recording on the last word. No sign-off, no "hope that helps" — she does not do one, and it is why the clip loops.
Add the three on-screen captions below in the Reels editor as you go. Do not use the auto-captions on their own; the numbers need to land as text.

videoGuides.hook: Start already on the claim, looking down the lens. No greeting, no name, no "so a lot of you have been asking". First words out: "Three reasons your colour looks flat right now."
shots: 0.0–4.0s — Propped phone, you from the chest up, salon behind. Say the opening line. Do not smile into it.
4.0–11.0s — Same frame, no cut. Reason one: ducted heating drying the cuticle so it stops reflecting light.
11.0–18.0s — Reason two: showers hotter than lukewarm, opening the cuticle and taking the toner with them.
18.0–26.0s — Reason three: stretching to eight or nine weeks because it is under a beanie anyway. Then stop recording mid-breath.
videoGuides.audio: Your own voice, no music. Freddie has no track under his either — a talking-head with a trending song over it reads as an ad. Film away from the dryer.

caption.hook: Three reasons your colour looks flat right now.
caption.body:
It's not you, and it's not the colour I put in. Winter does this every year.

Heating running all day dries the cuticle so it stops reflecting light. Showers hotter than lukewarm open it further and take your toner with them. And most people stretch to eight or nine weeks through winter, because nobody's seeing it under a beanie anyway.

All three are fixable in one appointment.

videoGuides.watchFor: The instinct is to open with "hi guys, so a lot of people ask me this". Freddie never does, and that is the whole reason his clip survives the first two seconds. Start on the claim.

videoGuides.title: Four things winter did to your hair
videoGuides.difficulty: Easy. Your own hair or a client already in the chair. Phone propped, one take, hands in the hair. No editing beyond captions.

copyThis.creator: hailey graham
copyThis.whatItIs: A stylist walking through four named types of hair damage, one at a time, holding hair to camera as she names each. Numbered, diagnostic, and built so the viewer is looking for themselves in the list.
copyThis.whyItCopies: A numbered damage explainer is the most forwarded shape in this niche, because the viewer is not just learning — they are sorting themselves into one of the categories, and then sending it to somebody they have diagnosed. That is the DM share, which is the strongest signal a Reel makes and something this account has never deliberately asked for.
howToCopy: Watch it once and count how long she spends on each of the four. It is roughly even, and none of them run long — that pacing is the format.
Note that she holds actual hair up while naming each one. Do not talk over a static shot of your face; the hair has to be in frame.
Prop the phone. Start on your hands lifting a dry mid-length section into the light, before you say a word.
Name your four in order: ducted heating, showers hotter than lukewarm, friction where the beanie sits, treatments skipped because it is not summer.
Swap her generic "heat damage" for the Melbourne-specific version. Ducted heating and beanies are what makes this yours rather than a repost of hers.
End on the line that earns the share: three of the four are fixable before spring. Then ask for the send in the caption, not out loud.

alsoWatch.creator: The Mane Choice
alsoWatch.what: Seasonal-breakage version with a trichologist explaining why hair breaks more in the cold months. Northern hemisphere, so their autumn is your August — the mechanism transfers, the season name does not.

alsoWatch.creator: KASEY LEE
alsoWatch.what: Same diagnostic shape run on one real client in the chair, if you would rather do it on a head than on your own hair.

references.what: Primary format reference — four named types of damage, verified live

videoGuides.hook: First half second is your hands lifting a section of dry mid-length into the light, before you say anything. Then: "If you have had a beanie on since June, this is you."
shots: 0.0–2.0s — Close on the hands, lifting a section. No face yet. This frame has to show the texture.
2.0–10.0s — Pull back to you in frame, still holding the section. One and two: ducted heating, showers too hot.
10.0–20.0s — Three and four: friction where the beanie sits, and treatments skipped because it is not summer.
20.0–28.0s — Drop the section, look at the lens: "Three of those four are fixable before spring." Stop.
onScreenText: 23.0s — Three of the four are fixable
videoGuides.audio: Your voice, with a quiet trending track underneath at low volume. Most of the feed watches on mute, so the on-screen text carries the four points and the voice is for whoever turns it on.

caption.hook: Send this to the friend who has been wearing a beanie since June.
caption.body:
Winter damage doesn't turn up as damage. It turns up as colour that goes flat faster than it used to, and ends that won't hold a tone.

Four things did it: ducted heating, showers hotter than lukewarm, friction where the beanie sits, and treatments skipped because it isn't summer. Three of those four are fixable before spring.

If you know exactly whose hair I just described, send it to her.

videoGuides.watchFor: If the first frame is your face instead of hair, the send-me mechanism breaks — people forward a clip about hair, not a clip of a person talking. Lead with the section in your hand.

videoGuides.title: Where the paint actually goes
videoGuides.difficulty: Moderate. Needs a balayage client and the phone propped over your shoulder. Silent, so it can be filmed on a busy day without breaking the appointment.

copyThis.creator: Alfredo Lewis
copyThis.whatItIs: Close, over-the-shoulder shots of freehand balayage being painted on, letting whole brush strokes play out uncut, then cutting to the finished blow-dry. No talking.
copyThis.whyItCopies: Technique footage is what someone researching a service watches before they book, and it does something a finished photo cannot — it makes the time visible. That is the missing half of Tuesday's $340 post: a price only reads as fair once you have watched where the three and a half hours goes. It is also silent, so it survives a busy day.
howToCopy: Watch how long he holds a single stroke. Most stylists cut every half second; he does not, and that is why it reads as skill rather than as an edit.
Prop the phone over your shoulder, close enough that the section fills the frame. Do not shoot the whole head.
Open on the brush already loaded and touching the hair. No mixing bowl, no gloves going on, no setup.
Film three or four separate strokes on different sections. You only need one good one, but you will not know which until you look.
Get one shot that clearly shows the gap you leave at the root. That gap is the entire argument of the video and it is the thing clients do not know about.
Cut straight to the finished blow-dry in window light. One slow pan down the length. No turn to camera, no smile.

alsoWatch.creator: The Edgycator
alsoWatch.what: Explains painting in V and W shapes and why the shape matters. Useful if you would rather talk over the technique than run it silent.

alsoWatch.creator: dvcolour
alsoWatch.what: Step-by-step surface-painting balayage on a brunette, leaving the natural root out. Closest to a lived-in blonde on darker hair.

references.what: Primary format reference — freehand balayage painting, uncut strokes, verified live
Painting shape explained on camera, verified live

videoGuides.hook: Open on the brush already loaded and touching the hair. The first frame is pigment meeting a section — no bowl, no gloves, no preamble.
shots: 0.0–4.0s — Over-shoulder, close. One brush stroke laying colour down a section. Let the whole stroke play out uncut.
4.0–8.0s — Same angle, a section further back. Show the gap left at the root clearly.
8.0–13.0s — Pull back slightly so three finished sections sit together and the placement reads as a pattern, not one stripe.
13.0–18.0s — Cut to the blow-dried finish in window light. One slow pan down the length.
onScreenText: 5.0s — The gap at the root is deliberate
9.0s — This is why it grows out soft
videoGuides.audio: Trending audio from the Reels tab that day, at full volume. There is no speech in this one, so the track is doing the retention work.

caption.hook: The gap I leave at the root is the whole reason it grows out soft.
caption.body:
Hand-painted colour goes where the light would naturally hit, and it stops short of the root on purpose. That gap is what stops you getting a hard line in eight weeks.

It's slower than foils and it isn't the cheaper option. It's the one you want if you'd rather come back in four months than in six.

videoGuides.watchFor: Do not film the mixing bowl. Every salon films the bowl and it is the part nobody watches — Alfredo starts on the hair and so should you.
